Re: Testimony of MCCA regarding LD 1114, An Act to Provide That Spouses and Children of Corrections Officers Who Die in the Line of Duty Receive a Pension
Chair Beebe-Center, Chair Hasenfus, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety:
On behalf of the Maine County Commissioners Association, we appreciate the opportunity to provide testimony to this Committee neither for nor against LD 1114. We recognize that similar survivor benefits appear to exist for other types of law enforcement personnel, and life insurance-related benefits for children and spouses appear to be in place for county correction officers.
About MCCA. Briefly, the Maine County Commissioners Association was established in 1890 to assist Maine's county government in providing vital services to Maine citizens in a responsive, efficient, and credible manner. The Association is based in Augusta, represents all 16 of Maine's counties, and is governed by a board with representation from each participating county.
What does LD 1114 do? LD 1114 would provide that the surviving spouses and children of corrections officers, including county corrections officers, who die in the line of duty receive a pension. The bill seeks to align benefits for corrections officers with those available to other law enforcement personnel who face similar risks.
LD 1114 creates a new benefit applicable to county corrections officers. LD 1114 creates a new pension benefit for the families of county corrections officers that already applies to many law enforcement officers. This benefit appears in statute at entitled: "Death benefits for law enforcement officers, firefighters, emergency medical services persons, department of corrections law enforcement officers and corrections officers who die while in the line of duty." 25 M.R.S. �1612 Further, there is a specific statute applying such benefits to sheriffs in statute at 30-A M.R.S. �352.
Separately, the Department of Corrections has established a program applicable to county corrections officers that provides life insurance benefits to the surviving spouses or children when the officer dies in the line of duty. See MDOC Policy, Line of Duty Death Benefit for Corrections Officers & MDOC Law Enforcement Officers, Policy Number 3.32.

Testimony of MCCA re LD 1114 May 12, 2025 Page 2
We are not opposed to the concept of expanding Maine law to require a pension for surviving spouses or children of county corrections officers who die in the line of duty. County corrections officers perform important services in often difficult conditions, and it is important that they and their families are appropriately compensated for their work and the risks they take.
Mandate preamble required. The cost of operating county jail services is primarily borne by local property taxpayers. Currently, the State contributes under 20% of the annual cost of operating county jails, leaving the remainder to come from local property taxpayers. Local property taxpayers are burdened with the cost of operating county jails even though the primary cost driver of county jails flows from the state's criminal justice system, including: the adoption of state laws criminalizing activities; charging decisions by state prosecutors; arrests by the state police; actions by the Department of Corrections to establish minimum operational standards of jails; and decisions made by Maine's courts to levy bail, convict, and sentence defendants.
To the extent LD 1114 establishes a new program that has a cost, it would be considered a local "mandate" under the Maine Constitution. As a result, the State would be responsible for 90% of the costs of this new program unless this legislation is adopted with 2/3 support with a mandate preamble.
Conclusion. We appreciate the Committee's attention to this issue and welcome further discussion on how best to support corrections officers and their families while ensuring fiscal responsibility at the county level. If you have questions or need additional information, please do not hesitate to let us know.
Respectfully submitted,

Stephen Gorden Co-Chair, Legislative Policy Committee, MCCA

Jean-Marie Caterina Co-Chair, Legislative Policy Committee, MCCA

Testimony ofRep. Sue Salisbury presenting
LD 1114, An Act to Provide That Spouses and Children of Corrections Officers Who Die in the Line of Duty Receive a Pension
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safiety
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and esteemed members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety, I am Sue Salisbury, and I represent House District 128, which includes part of Westbrook. I am here today to present my final bill of this
session, LD 1114, An Act to Provide that Spouses and Children of Corrections Officers Who Die in the Line of Duty Receive a Pension.
I want to thank you all for your time and attention to all of the bills that I have presented before
you this session. A few have been bills that I have worked on for more than one session, and a
few, like this one, are bills that I am giving my first try at.
This is another bill that was brought to me by Sheriff Joyce. This bill would add corrections
officers to the provision of law that deals with line-of-duty deaths. The bill would require that
spouses or children of corrections officers who die as a result of an injury received in the line of
duty must receive pensions equal to `/2 of the pay of the corrections officer but not less than $1,000 annually.
I am the wife of a retired corrections officer, who was raising four children with him at the time
he was employed. We both feared that something would happen to him on the job, and I knew
that if something had happened to him, we would be emotionally and financially devastated. Corrections officers know the danger that they face in their line of work, and they accept that when they take the job. However, they should not have to be worrying about what will happen to
their families if they become seriously injured or even killed in the line of duty.
This bill is another step toward acknowledging the stressful and dangerous work that corrections officers do, and it provides a little peace of mind to the families of the corrections officers.
Thank you again for your consideration of all my bills this session. I am happy to answer any
questions you may have, but I may defer to Sheriff Joyce, who is here as well.

RE: LD1114 --AN ACT TO PROVIDE THAT SPOUSES AND CHILDREN OF CORRECTIONS OFFICERS WHO
DIE IN THE LINE OF DUTY RECEIVE A PENSION.

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and Distinguished Legislative Members of the Criminal Justice and Public
Safety Committee;

My name is William Doyle. Currently I serve in the role of Executive Director for the National Correctional Employees Unions
(NCEU). The National Correctional Employees Union (NCEU) represents nine (9) County Correctional Units in the State of Maine comprising of approx. four hundred (400) members from York to Aroostook County.

The NCEU rises in favor and wholeheartedly supports LD1114 and commends Representative Salisbury for submitting
legislation aimed at tackling several issues near and dear to the corrections profession. The current proposed piece of legislation will provide a much needed safety net for families of correctional officers who die in the Line of Duty. According to an article from the American Correctional Officer Intelligence Network, now One Voice United, the average life expectancy of a corrections officer is 59 years of age. (ACOIN, 2015) Corrections officers suffer from higher PTSD, suicide, and divorce rates
than other professions and the general public. Please See ACOIN publication, Impacts of Understaffing, (March 2017) and
Desert Waters Correctional Outreach study (2013). People who enter jails are often stressed, combative, and under the influence. These factors lead to altercations which place correctional employees in harms way day in and day out. Not only are correctional employees forced into physical altercations to protect themselves or others, they are ofien exposed to bodily fluids
such as saliva, urine, and feces being used as weapons.
The County jail system has been financially handcuffed ever since the jail consolidation efforts of 2008. The NCEU submitted
testimony in favor of LD's 852 and respectively 719 aimed at increasing state funding for the County Jail Operations Fund. Due
to the fiscal challenges, collective bargaining for wages and benefits suffered concessions which negatively affected staffing levels at all prisons and jails. Currently, Cumberland County has approx.70 vacancies and York County has approx. 28 vacancies for corrections officers. Staffing shortages cause increases in voluntary and mandated overtime. Unlike other
professions, Correctional Staff do not have the ability to say, "No" to mandated overtime. In fact, Correctional Officers have
been disciplined for refusing to stay for overtime.
Due to the increased demand on Correctional Officers and inherent dangers of the profession previously identified, LD 1114
will make sure that spouse's or minor children will receive half (1/2) of the Off1cer's pay as a pension benefit, but no less than $1,000 annually. Ensuring that their families are supported financially should they die in the Line of Duty is morally ethical and a testament to the value we place on the profession. Support of this legislation by Senators and Representatives will show parity with fellow law enforcement officers who currently receive this benefit.

In closing, the NCEU would like to reiterate our support for LD1114 and urge the committee and full legislature pass this
important piece of legislation. Thank you very mucl1 for your time and I'm happy to field any questions.
WM In Solidarity, rl ram Doyle
